slides.heading: Compound (Reflexive) Pronouns
bullets: Add -self or -selves to a personal pronoun:  myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself.
Plural forms:  ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
Use them to turn the action back on the doer:  “She hurt herself.”
Or for emphasis:  “I myself saw it.”

slides.heading: Practice — Which Reflexive Pronoun?
slides.instruction: Fill each blank with the right reflexive pronoun.

slides.heading: Pronoun Cautions
bullets: Use who as a subject, whom as an object:  “the man who spoke,” “the man whom I saw.”
Ask “who?” for the doer, “whom?” for the receiver:  “Who called?”  “Whom did you call?”
Put the persons in order — you and I, he and I (name yourself last).
Make a pronoun agree with its antecedent in gender, person, and number.

slides.heading: Practice — Who or Whom?
slides.instruction: Choose who or whom for each blank.

slides.heading: Double Relatives
bullets: Some relatives contain both the antecedent and the relative in one word.
what = “that which”:  “I got what I wanted” = “the thing which I wanted.”
whoever = “he who”:  “Whoever runs may read” = “he who runs may read.”
These are called Double Relatives — they do two jobs at once.

slides.heading: Comparison of Adjectives
bullets: Adjectives change form to show different degrees of a quality.
Positive — the simple quality:  tall, rich, beautiful.
Comparative — compares two:  taller, richer, more beautiful.
Superlative — the highest among three or more:  tallest, richest, most beautiful.

slides.heading: Forming the Degrees
bullets: Short words — add -er, -est:  tall, taller, tallest.
Longer words — use more, most:  careful, more careful, most careful.
Irregular:  good, better, best;  bad, worse, worst;  little, less, least;  many, more, most.
A few cannot be compared:  square, round, perfect, dead.

slides.heading: Practice — Which Degree?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each adjective is positive, comparative, or superlative.

slides.heading: Kinds of Definitive Adjectives
bullets: Demonstratives point out:  this, that, these, those.
Distributives take one at a time:  each, every, either, neither.
Indefinites are vague in amount:  all, any, some, few, many, several, no.
Numerals count or order:  cardinal (one, two), ordinal (first, second), multiplicative (double, triple).

slides.heading: Practice — Which Kind of Definitive?
slides.instruction: Tell whether each is demonstrative, distributive, indefinite, or numeral.

slides.heading: Adjective Cautions
bullets: Never double a comparison:  “taller,” not “more taller”; “tallest,” not “most tallest.”
Put the ordinal before the cardinal:  “the first four,” not “the four first.”
Match number:  “this kind,” “these kinds” — a plural adjective with a plural noun.
Some adjectives are already complete and take no more, most, or -er:  round, perfect.
